narration: Cocoa butter can freeze into six different solids, and only one feels right.

Chocolate tastes so good largely because of how it melts and what that melt releases: cocoa butter, tempered into a crystal form that melts at about 34 degrees Celsius, stays solid in your hand and turns liquid on your tongue, carrying aroma built during fermentation and roasting up to your nose.
The six forms were mapped with X-ray diffraction, in work published through the American Oil Chemists' Society.
But that number explains texture, not flavour, and it says nothing about why anyone likes it.
Those are separate questions, answered by separate instruments, and one of them is barely answered at all.
Why does chocolate taste so good?
Start with the moment of eating, because that is where the physics is easiest to see.
A square of well-made dark chocolate snaps cleanly. Held in a warm palm for a minute it softens, but on the tongue it collapses into liquid within seconds.
That contrast is not luck. Cocoa butter, the fat pressed from cacao beans, has a melting range that sits just under the temperature inside your mouth.
Solid on the shelf, solid in the hand, liquid in the mouth: a narrow window, and good chocolate lives inside it.
Melting is a phase change, not a chemical reaction, and it takes energy.
As the fat turns from solid to liquid it draws heat from your tongue, which is part of why tempered chocolate can feel faintly cool as it goes.
The liquid fat then coats the mouth, and with it come sugar, cocoa solids and the volatile molecules that carry aroma.
Texture comes first, and texture is the delivery system for everything else.
A chocolate that melts too high feels waxy and holds its flavour back. One that melts too low goes soft in the wrapper.
Here is the part that surprises people. Cocoa butter is not one solid.
Its fat molecules, mostly triglycerides, can stack together in several different crystal arrangements, a property called polymorphism.
The molecules are the same; only the packing changes. Different packing means a different melting point, a different hardness and a different surface.
The standard scheme, published in the Journal of the American Oil Chemists' Society and still the reference point in confectionery science, describes six forms, numbered One to Six.

The way chemists tell these forms apart is X-ray diffraction. A beam of X-rays passed through a crystalline sample scatters off the regular layers of molecules, and the angles of the scattered beams reveal how far apart those layers are.
Each form leaves its own pattern, a kind of fingerprint for packing.

Paired with an instrument that measures how much heat a sample absorbs as it warms, known as differential scanning calorimetry, the patterns let researchers match each crystal arrangement to its melting behaviour.
Nobody had to taste their way to this result. It was measured.
Of the six, Form Five is the one chocolate makers want. It melts at about 34 degrees Celsius, it is hard enough to snap, and it sets with a glossy surface.
The lower forms melt too easily and feel greasy. Form Six is more stable still, but it forms slowly, over long storage, and as it does the surface turns dull and the texture grainy.
That is why the number in the cold open matters: it is the melting point of one specific crystal, not of cocoa butter in general.
Left to cool on its own, melted chocolate sets into a mixture of forms, and the result is soft, streaky and dull.
Tempering is the fix. First the chocolate is heated until every existing crystal is gone.
Then it is cooled, so crystals begin to form. Then it is warmed slightly, just enough to melt the unstable forms while the Form Five crystals survive.
Those survivors act as seeds, and as the chocolate sets they template the rest of the fat into the same arrangement.
Professionals do it on marble slabs or in machines; the principle is the same.
When tempering fails, or when a bar is stored warm, you can see it.
Grey-white streaks and a dusty film appear on the surface. This is fat bloom, and it is often mistaken for mould.
It is fat recrystallising, frequently into Form Six, scattering light instead of reflecting it.
It is a change in structure, not something growing. But the melt changes, and so does the eating.
The bloom is visible proof that crystal form is part of what you taste.
What are people repeating without checking? What's hidden by the way the story is usually told?
The tongue detects a short list of basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savoury.
Chocolate certainly registers on that list, mostly as sweet and bitter. But the character people mean when they say chocolate, the roasted, fruity, nutty, sometimes floral quality, is aroma.
Volatile molecules released by the melting fat travel up the back of the throat to the nose.
This route is called retronasal smell, and it is why chocolate tastes flat when your nose is blocked.
You can notice it yourself by pinching your nostrils while a piece melts, then letting go.

So how do chemists find out which molecules carry that aroma? A chocolate extract is fed through a gas chromatograph, which separates a mixture into its components as they travel through a long, thin column at different speeds.
At the end, the stream is split. Part goes to a detector, often a mass spectrometer that identifies the molecule.
Part goes to a sniffing port, where a trained person records what each component smells like and how strongly.
This is gas chromatography–olfactometry, and the human nose is part of the instrument.
Results of this kind appear regularly in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry.
What this work shows is that no single molecule smells like chocolate.
Chemists have identified a large number of volatile compounds in cocoa, and estimates of how many vary with the method and with what counts as present.
Only a fraction of them reach a level the nose can detect, and the impression of chocolate comes from their combination.
Remove one and the picture shifts. Some of the important ones, smelled alone, would not remind you of chocolate at all.
Fresh cacao beans taste nothing like chocolate. They are bitter and astringent, packed inside a pod in sweet white pulp.
After harvest, beans and pulp are heaped or boxed and left for several days.
Yeasts ferment the sugars in the pulp, then bacteria turn the products into lactic and acetic acid.
Heat builds, the acids enter the bean, and the bean's internal structure breaks down.
Its own enzymes begin cutting proteins into smaller pieces and splitting sugars.
Those fragments are flavour precursors: they do not yet smell of chocolate, but without them roasting has little to work with.
Roasting is where the precursors pay off. Heated together, amino acids and reducing sugars undergo the Maillard reaction, the same family of reactions that browns bread crust and seared meat.
It produces a cascade of new molecules, among them pyrazines, which carry roasted and nutty notes.
Researchers established the role of fermentation partly by comparison: beans dried without proper fermentation and then roasted develop only weak chocolate aroma.
The farm, in other words, writes much of the recipe before the beans ever reach a factory.
After roasting, the beans are cracked, the shells removed, and the nibs ground into a paste.
Sugar and often extra cocoa butter are added, the mixture is ground until the particles are too fine for the tongue to notice as grit, and then it is conched: stirred and kneaded for hours.
Conching lets some harsh, volatile acids escape and coats every solid particle in fat.
That coating is why smooth chocolate feels smooth. Once again, texture and flavour turn out not to be separable.
Chocolate is not only sweet. Cacao contains theobromine, a bitter compound closely related to caffeine, along with polyphenols that taste bitter and feel astringent, a drying pull on the mouth.
Theobromine takes its name from the genus of the cacao tree, Theobroma, from the Greek for food of the gods.
Its structure and properties are catalogued in PubChem, the open chemistry database run by the National Institutes of Health.
Bitterness here is not a flaw to be removed. Makers balance it against sugar and fat, and that balance is much of what separates a dark bar from a milk one.

This is also why preference splits so sharply between people. The same chemistry reaches every tongue, but sensitivity to bitterness differs from person to person, and so does what someone grew up eating.
A bar one person finds richly complex, another finds harsh. Food science can describe the bar precisely. It cannot, from the bar alone, predict the verdict.
Now to what people repeat without checking. A popular story says chocolate tastes good because it contains special molecules that act on the brain, sometimes called a love chemical.
Some of the compounds named in that story are genuinely present in cocoa; that part checks out.
What has not been shown is that they reach the brain from an ordinary piece of chocolate in amounts that explain the pleasure.
How much liking is learned rather than triggered remains open. The story survives because it is simpler than the real one, which is a crystal, a melt, a nose and a long chain of processing.
Notice what the stronger explanation rests on. Crystal forms are measured by diffraction and calorimetry, in work published through the American Oil Chemists' Society.
Aroma compounds are separated by chromatography and confirmed by trained noses, in journals like the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry.
The bitter compounds are catalogued in PubChem. Each step has an instrument behind it, and each step can be checked by someone else repeating it.
The pleasure molecule story has none of that chain. It has a plausible name and a satisfying shape.
When the cross-section of tempered chocolate appears, watch the packing, not the colour.
The glow marks the Form Five crystals, the ordered layers that diffraction measures.
The animation is a model, not a microscope image; real crystals are far smaller and far less tidy.
The degree counter earlier showed one temperature only, about 34 degrees Celsius, because that is the one figure this episode can source.
Everything else, from roasting heat to conching time, varies with the maker, and the graphics leave it out on purpose.
Be clear about what this evidence does not establish. It explains why chocolate melts the way it does, where much of its aroma comes from, and why processing changes the result.
It does not explain why a particular person loves it, or why liking differs across people and places.
Those are questions about perception, memory and culture, and the instruments in this episode do not measure them.
Nothing here says anything about chocolate and health; that is a different body of evidence, and not one this episode examined.

So the next square you eat is doing something precise. A crystal chosen by tempering gives way just below the heat of your mouth, and the fat releases molecules built by microbes and a roaster, long before and far away. The pleasure is yours. The melt, at least, has been measured.
